steps.title: can / could
steps.html:
NowIn the past
PositiveYou can buy it online.You could talk to the shop assistant.
NegativeYou can't use euros in Norway.You couldn't buy petrol at supermarkets.
QuestionCan you drive?Could you swim at five?
Short answerYes, I can. / No, I can't.Yes, I could. / No, I couldn't.

After can and could the verb has no to and no -s.

The form is the same for every person: I can, she can, they can.

can covers both what you are able to do and what is possible.

Learners often write She cans swim or I can to swim. Both are wrong.

steps.title: You are going to read about shopping then and now.
steps.sub: Which do you think was better?

steps.title: 1 · Then
steps.html:
Thirty years ago you couldn't buy everything in one place. You went to the baker's for bread and to the butcher's for meat, and you couldn't do any of it after six o'clock. You couldn't pay by card in a small shop and you certainly couldn't order anything on the internet.

But you could talk. The shop assistant knew your name, and you could ask her anything. Shopping took an hour, and for a lot of people that hour was the only time they could chat to somebody.

steps.title: 2 · Now
steps.html:
Today you can buy bread, meat, petrol and a phone in the same building, at eleven at night. You can order almost anything online and it can arrive the next morning. It's cheap and it's easy.

But there are things the internet can't do. It can't cut your hair and it can't give you a cup of coffee. So the old shops closed, and now there are five cafés and three hairdresser's on the same street. People still can't buy everything online — and they still want to talk.
